Q: How to fix ARM link failure from warning: creating DT_TEXTREL in a PIE? A:

I think this is a toolchain configuration issue caused by a change in newer Gentoo toolchains.

The failure is the result of two things happening together:

  • GCC 15 on Gentoo enables PIE by default for the aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu profile.

  • Newer binutils releases (2.43 and later) promote DT_TEXTREL in a PIE from a warning to a link-time error. You’re using binutils 2.46, which enforces this.

TF-A BL31 is an EL3 firmware image that executes from a fixed physical address. It is not a userspace executable and must not be built as a PIE. There is no dynamic loader available to resolve runtime relocations, so a PIE build is fundamentally incorrect for BL31.

You have a couple of options:

Option 1: Use an older toolchain

The simplest workaround is to use GCC 14 (or earlier), which does not enable PIE by default for this target.

crossdev --stable -t aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu --gcc 14

Option 2: Explicitly disable PIE

If you want to stay on GCC 15, pass flags that disable PIE generation:

make V=1 -j4 \
  CROSS_COMPILE=aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu- \
  CFLAGS="-fno-pie -fno-pic" \
  LDFLAGS="-no-pie" \
  ARCH=aarch64 PLAT=k3 SPD=opteed \
  K3_USART=0x6 BL32_BASE=0x80080000 PRELOADED_BL33_BASE=0x82000000 \
  TARGET_BOARD=lite all

You can verify whether PIE is being injected by checking the verbose build output (V=1) and looking for -fPIE, -fpie, or -pie in the compiler/linker command lines.

Once PIE is disabled, the DT_TEXTREL error should disappear and BL31 should link normally.

Q: Do C++ projects break when trying to launch on other distros? A:

It depends on what libraries (and what versions thereof) you use. A good rule of thumb is: if you compile your code on a distro from 3 years ago, it will run on any normal distro of today. Since not everybody uses a "distro of today" there is a bit of value in compiling on a distro 5-7 years old, but it's often not necessary.

If you need newer libraries than the 3-year-old distro provides, DO NOT USE STATIC LINKING - it breaks all sorts of things in subtle ways. Instead, the proper solution is to bundle your libraries in an adjacent directory and use a relative RPATH. There's some FUD about "RPATH bad" floating around the internet, but it only applies if you are writing a privileged program (setuid, setcap, etc.) and such programs should be tightly coupled to the distro anyway (and even then, an absolute non-world-writable directory can still be used safely).

Note however that ABI concerns are not the only portability issue, just the most glaring one. Such other portability problems are one of the reasons static linking breaks things.

Q: How to determine if a caught fetch error is retryable? A:

While InDevX has a good mechanical description of how to retry, unfortunately the semantics of HTTP don't tell you if every operation is safe to retry. The behavior of the HTTP endpoint drives that decision. This means:

  • You cannot use the HTTP status code to know something is safe to retry.
  • Some HTTP methods, like GET, are typically safe to retry.
  • Any DELETE, POST or PUT operation might or might not be safe — check the developer API documentation.
  • You might need to inspect the response body or response headers to see if the API declares whether or not you can retry the request; again this all depends on the API, not the HTTP spec.

The HTTP spec defines safe methods as only those that are essentially read-only; no modification of data is considered "safe", and therefore "safe to retry."

You can infer that some operations are unsafe to retry. For example, a POST to perform a payment is not safe to retry, no matter what error you get from the backend if the response does not explicitly say you can retry the request. Retrying a payment request can result in duplicate charges, which is not a good thing. GET requests are supposed to be idempotent according to the HTTP spec; that should be safe to retry. A DELETE request to get rid of a resource is probably safe to retry; after all, the worse case outcome is the thing you tried to delete is already gone. It's hard to see that as an error; it's "mission accomplished."

So, there's no clear-cut answer to your question. The spec says read-only requests are safe (and safe to retry), but the behavior of a specific endpoint can either be safe to retry, or not. You'll need to check with the maintainers of those endpoints to get an authoritative answer.

Some additional posts on Stack Overflow that you might find interesting related to this topic:

  • What is idempotency in HTTP methods?
  • How does concepts idempotent and safe methods differ?
  • Is it safe to use PUT and DELETE requests
  • Idempotentency of GET verb in an RESTful API
  • Which HTTP errors should never trigger an automatic retry?
  • How to retry HTTP POST requests

Q: Algorithm to check if byte is 0x00 or 0xFF A:

You can use an arithmetic (signed) shift to the right. When comparing, cast the types to one: char or unsigned char to avoid integer promotion:

((char)i >> 1) == (char)i

or

(unsigned char)((char)i >> 1) == i

Moreover, the shift value does not have to be 1.
